Maladaptive Strategies.value: I dwell on how the event could have been prevented
I put on loud music or TV
Being around people in authority or uniform

Threat.value: I often react as if I am in danger even when nothing is actually wrong
Unexpected movement nearby causes me to react as if I am in danger
I always choose where to sit based on how safe or protected I feel

Memory.value: When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event.
When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop
My memories of the frightening event are very clear and detailed.

Negative Appraisals.value: The world is a dangerous place
People are not what they seem
I feel like I don't know myself anymore

issues.item: Triggers: Sexual Trauma Cues: Comments on sexual violence
issues.explanation: For a refugee trauma profile, comments on sexual violence are too trauma-specific and suggest a sexual assault formulation that is not otherwise supported by the threat, memory, or appraisal items. Nothing else in the profile indicates sexual trauma content, making this trigger hard to reconcile with the stated trauma type.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Evaluation: Situations in which other people evaluate me / my appearance / my performance
issues.explanation: Avoiding situations where others evaluate appearance/performance fits social-evaluative shame concerns, but the rest of the profile centers on danger, distrust, intrusive sensory recall, and hypervigilance rather than evaluation-based threat. This strategy is not well linked to the active trigger/threat/appraisal pattern and is clinically out of place.

vignette: When Luciana and her younger brother first crossed the border, the patrol guards did not merely detain them; they forced them into a windowless holding cell where the air hung thick with the sour tang of cheap liquor. When the shift commander barked orders to drop to the concrete, Luciana froze, her body obeying the command before her mind could process the violence. Years later, those exact cues still hijack her nervous system. When she catches the faint whiff of whiskey at the prison commissary or sees a correctional officer’s polished boots clacking down the tier, her triggers immediately fire false alarms, convincing her that the old detention room has materialized around her. Her body tenses, her breath quickens, and she startles violently at the sudden sway of a swinging door or the sharp intake of breath from a fellow guard. Those sudden cues do not just frighten her; they actively convince her that the world is fundamentally unsafe and that anyone in authority is secretly hiding violent intentions. That sudden certainty, in turn, forces her to flee the scene or retreat to a corner where she can back against the wall, constantly scanning for exits. As the months passed after her resettlement, the memories of that night refused to fade. When a clear and detailed image of the guard’s belt snapped across her mind, the sheer volume of her terror forced her to stop mid-sentence and turn on the television at maximum volume. The memory directly fed her sense of threat, causing her false alarms to spike and her body to brace for violence. The noise did not erase the image; it merely buried it, but the burial itself deepened her fear that she was losing herself and no longer knew who she was. Because she distrusted her own judgment now, she interpreted every glance from her husband or her supervisor as a prelude to betrayal. That growing distrust of others made her hyper-sensitive to any new command, which then intensified her trigger response. Her pervasive distrust also convinced her that avoidance was the only way to survive, which drove her to engage in preventive rumination and sensory distraction, as she decided she could not trust anyone to keep her safe. When the memories finally broke through her coping mechanisms, the overwhelming emotion usually drove her to replay hypotheticals of how she might have shielded her brother better. This mental loop convinced her that isolation was necessary, which led her to skip team briefings and refuse direct instructions from the wardens. By avoiding direct authority figures, she deprived herself of disconfirming data, which made her trigger threshold drop, so that minor cues suddenly felt dangerous. The habit of sensory blocking also solidified her negative appraisals, convincing her that she was fundamentally broken and that the world was inherently hostile. When she finally snapped off the radio in her kitchen, the silence that followed did not bring peace; it brought the smell of alcohol and the echo of the commander’s voice back into the room, which then triggered another surge of physiological threat and another wave of catastrophic thoughts. The cycle slowly eroded her marriage, as her husband learned that asking her to walk past a parking meter with a patrol car idling would send her into a cold sweat. At thirty-four, the cumulative weight of sleepless nights, the erosion of her professional authority, and the exhausting loop of predicting danger from harmless cues finally pushed her into a therapist’s office. She sits there now, hoping to stop the relentless turning of the wheel, terrified that one misstep will unravel the fragile safety she has built, yet clinging to the quiet hope that she might finally remember who she was before the world taught her to look for enemies in every shadow.
